How to Play Pizza Ready!

Pizza Ready! is an idle restaurant simulator: you are the owner, chef and busiest pair of hands in a growing pizzeria. The core loop is simple to learn — take orders, cook, serve, collect cash, upgrade — but running the shop well means keeping every part of it moving at once. Here is how a typical session flows.

1. Run your pizza shop

You start with a tiny shop, one oven and a counter. Walk over the glowing floor pads to interact with each station: stand by the oven to collect finished pizzas, carry them to the serving counter or to tables, and step on the cash piles customers leave behind to collect your earnings. Movement is everything — the faster you complete the loop, the faster money comes in.

2. Take and complete orders

Customers arrive with a bubble showing how many pizzas they want. Some queue at the counter for takeaway, some sit at tables to dine in, and later, cars pull up at the drive-thru window. Fill each order exactly, deliver it, and the customer pays and leaves happy. Served customers also fill your shop's star progress bar — fill it to complete the location.

Watch the queues: a long line at one station usually means a bottleneck somewhere else. If customers wait at the counter while pizzas sit ready, you need carrying capacity; if the counter is empty, your ovens are the problem.

3. Keep the kitchen producing

Pizzas come off the production line continuously, but only up to a stack limit. If the finished-pizza stack hits MAX and nobody collects it, production is wasted. Keep stacks moving to customers so the ovens never sit idle, and clear finished tables quickly so new guests can sit down.

4. Spend cash on upgrades

Every pizza sold earns cash, and cash is best spent the moment you can afford the next improvement. The main upgrade paths are:

  • Your character — carrying capacity and movement speed, so each trip moves more pizzas in less time.
  • Ovens & production — more output per minute and higher stack limits.
  • The shop floor — extra tables, extra registers and new areas such as the drive-thru.
  • Staff — hired helpers who run stations for you (see the Tips page for hiring strategy).

5. Complete the location and move on

Each restaurant has a set of goals shown on the progress bar at the top of the screen. Finishing them completes the shop and unlocks the next location, where you build again from a small start — but with bigger numbers, new layouts and fresh challenges. That cycle of build, complete and expand is the road to becoming a pizza tycoon.

New to the game? Read our Tips & Tricks next to earn faster from your very first shop.

Pizza Ready! Tips & Tricks

Small decisions compound quickly in an idle game. These are the habits that separate a shop that crawls from one that prints money.

Earn faster

Never let the oven stack sit at MAX

A full stack means production has stopped earning. Sweep past the oven on every trip around the shop so pizzas keep flowing to customers.

Collect floor cash promptly

Cash piles left on tables and the floor are money you cannot spend yet. Pick them up on your way between stations instead of making special trips.

Serve the shortest queue first

Quick orders keep customer turnover high. Clearing several small orders usually earns more per minute than one long delivery run.

Claim your offline earnings

Your staff keep working while you are away. Log in regularly, collect what they earned, and reinvest it immediately so the next offline period pays even more.

Upgrade in the right order

Capacity before speed

Carrying two extra pizzas per trip beats arriving slightly sooner with the same small stack. Raise capacity first, then movement speed.

Balance the chain

An idle game earns at the speed of its slowest station. If pizzas pile up uncooked, upgrade production; if they pile up cooked, upgrade serving and registers.

Tables and registers multiply income

Each new table or register is another customer paying at the same time. Unlock them as soon as your current spots are constantly full.

Save gems for permanent boosts

Premium currency is scarce. Spend it on lasting improvements rather than small one-time cash bundles you could earn in a few minutes of play.

Hiring staff

Hire cashiers early

A cashier frees you from standing at the register, letting you focus on cooking and delivery — the two jobs only you can rush.

Staff the bottleneck

Put your next hire wherever work piles up. A chef is best when ovens lag; a server is best when cooked pizzas wait undelivered.

Upgrade your best workers

A leveled-up employee at a busy station outperforms a fresh hire at a quiet one. Strengthen the stations that never stop.

Staff = offline income

Hired workers are what your shop earns with while the game is closed. A fully staffed shop makes coming back far more rewarding.

Expanding

Finish goals, don't just grind

The star progress bar is your map. Completing listed goals unlocks the next location faster than endlessly farming the current one.

Open the drive-thru as soon as you can

The drive-thru is a second, parallel stream of customers and cash. Unlocking it is one of the biggest single income jumps in a shop.

Reinvest in new locations quickly

In a fresh restaurant, early upgrades are cheap and pay back fast. Spend aggressively at the start of each new shop.

Check in daily

Daily check-ins and events hand out skins, boosts and currency. A minute a day keeps the bonuses — and your momentum — rolling.

Best Upgrades to Buy First in Pizza Ready

Every pizza you sell turns into cash, and every pile of cash presents the same question: what do I buy next? Pizza Ready! offers dozens of upgrades — ovens, counters, seats, your own speed and strength — but they do not all pay back at the same rate. Buy them in the right order and each purchase funds the next one sooner. Buy them in the wrong order and your shop crawls while expensive equipment sits half-used. This guide ranks the early upgrades by how fast they return their cost.

Start with the bottleneck, not the wishlist

Your shop earns at the speed of its slowest step. Pizzas have to be baked, carried, served and paid for, in that order, and money only arrives at the end of the chain. Before buying anything, watch one full minute of play and ask where things pile up. If finished pizzas stack up at the oven with nobody collecting them, baking is not your problem — carrying is. If the counter queue is long but the oven stack is empty, the opposite is true. The best first upgrade is always the one that clears the current jam.

1. Carrying capacity — the fastest payback in the game

Your character is the only worker who can do every job, and early on you do almost all of them yourself. Every trip between the oven and the counter moves a fixed number of pizzas, so raising your carrying capacity raises the value of every single trip. Going from carrying four pizzas to six is a 50 percent increase in what one run delivers, with no extra walking. Capacity upgrades are cheap at the start and pay for themselves within a few minutes of play, which is why they come first on this list.

2. Movement speed — more trips per minute

Once you can carry a decent stack, speed is next. A faster character completes the oven–counter–table loop more often, collects floor cash sooner and reaches the drive-thru before drivers lose patience. Speed and capacity multiply each other: capacity decides how much each trip is worth, speed decides how many trips you make. Keep the two roughly level with each other rather than maxing one and ignoring the other.

3. Ovens — only as fast as you can serve

Oven upgrades raise how many pizzas come off the line and how high the finished stack can pile before production stalls. They matter enormously — but only once you and your staff can actually move the pizzas the ovens already produce. A common early trap is buying a second or third oven upgrade while finished pizzas sit at MAX waiting for collection: that cash would have earned far more as capacity or a cashier. Rule of thumb: if the oven stack regularly hits its limit, stop upgrading ovens and upgrade the serving side instead.

4. Counters and registers — more customers paying at once

Each register is a parallel checkout. With one counter, customers pay one at a time no matter how fast you cook; with two, your income ceiling roughly doubles during busy periods. Unlock extra counters as soon as your single queue is consistently full and your oven can keep up. Registers pair naturally with cashiers — a second counter with nobody staffing it still needs you standing there, so plan the hire that goes with it (our Staff Guide covers the order).

5. Seats and tables — turning queues into diners

Seated customers are patient customers. Tables convert people who would otherwise wait in line — or leave — into diners who order, eat and pay at a steady pace, and a cleared table immediately seats the next guest. Extra seating pays back fastest when your dine-in area is constantly full and guests are waiting for a free chair. If tables sit empty while the takeaway counter is swamped, spend on the counter side first and come back for seats later.

6. The drive-thru — a second shop in the same building

When it unlocks, the drive-thru adds an entirely separate stream of customers who never enter the dining room. It is one of the largest single income jumps available in a location, but it also spreads you thinner: somebody has to serve that window. Unlock it when your main floor runs smoothly with staff help, not before — a drive-thru you cannot service just creates a second queue of unhappy customers.

A simple buying order for a new shop

  • Carrying capacity, two or three levels.
  • Movement speed, to match.
  • First cashier hire, so the register never waits for you.
  • Oven output, until the stack rarely empties.
  • Second counter or register, with staff to run it.
  • Extra tables while dine-in is full.
  • Drive-thru, once the floor is staffed and stable.

The one-minute test: after any upgrade, watch the shop for a minute. If the pile-up you targeted has moved somewhere else, you bought correctly — the new pile-up is simply your next purchase. If nothing changed, the upgrade was not the bottleneck, and the cash would have worked harder elsewhere.

Upgrades decide how fast your shop can earn. How fast it actually earns depends on how you play — see How to Earn Money Faster in Pizza Ready for the habits that go with this buying order, or browse all articles.

How to Earn Money Faster in Pizza Ready

Two players can own identical shops and earn at completely different rates. The difference is rarely the upgrades — it is what happens minute to minute: how quickly orders are served, how happy customers stay, and how wisely the game's rewarded ads are used. This guide covers the active-play habits that raise your income per minute, in the shop you already have.

Serving speed is income

Money in Pizza Ready! arrives when a customer pays, and customers pay when their order is complete. Everything that shortens the gap between a customer arriving and paying puts cash in your hand sooner — and cash in hand buys the upgrades that make the next order faster still. In practice that means working in tight loops: collect from the oven, serve the counter, clear a table, sweep up floor cash, and be back at the oven as the next batch lands. Avoid crossing the shop for a single pizza when a full stack will be ready in three seconds; one trip carrying eight pizzas beats four trips carrying two.

Order matters too. Serve the customer who has waited longest when queues are similar in size, but if one order needs a single pizza and another needs six, clearing the small order first usually pays sooner and frees a spot for the next arrival. Watch order bubbles as you move and plan your route around them instead of reacting to whichever customer you happen to pass.

Happy customers pay, waiting customers leave

Customers have patience, and it drains while they wait — in the queue, at a dirty table, or at the drive-thru window. A customer who waits too long is lost income: the pizzas they would have bought are never sold, and the time you spent cooking them earns nothing. Keeping the shop happy is mostly about preventing extremes:

  • Never let one queue grow while another sits empty. A long line at the counter while tables stand clear means your serving is the bottleneck, not your cooking.
  • Clear finished tables quickly. A table that needs clearing seats nobody. Treat clearing as part of the serving loop, not an afterthought.
  • Keep the drive-thru moving. Drivers cannot see your busy dining room — they only see their own wait. A quick trip to the window between oven runs protects that whole income stream.
  • Watch the star progress bar. Served, satisfied customers fill it. If it barely moves while the shop looks busy, customers are leaving unserved somewhere.

Rewarded ads: powerful, if you spend them well

Pizza Ready! offers optional rewarded ads — short videos that grant bonuses such as temporary income multipliers or extra cash. They are genuinely useful, but their value depends entirely on when you take them:

  • Take income multipliers when the shop is at full speed. A double-income boost during your busiest, best-staffed minutes multiplies a big number. The same boost while your ovens are half-upgraded multiplies a small one.
  • Boost before a busy stretch, not after. Activate multipliers at the start of an active session, when you will personally keep every station flowing for the full duration.
  • Double offline earnings selectively. When you return to a large offline payout, doubling it can be the best-value ad in the game. When the payout is small, you may prefer to save your attention for a bigger one later (see how idle earnings work).
  • Do not let ads interrupt a rush. Thirty seconds away while queues build and customers leave can cost more than the reward pays. If the shop is straining, serve first and take the offer when things calm down.
  • Skip rewards you do not need. A small instant-cash offer is worth little if your next upgrade costs twenty times as much and you are earning well. Time is a resource too.

Reinvest immediately

Cash sitting in your balance earns nothing. The moment you can afford the upgrade that clears your current bottleneck, buy it — every minute spent saving "just in case" is a minute earning at the old, slower rate. The only exception is saving for a large unlock, like a new area or a key hire, that you are close to affording; then a short, deliberate save is a plan, not hesitation. Our guide to the best upgrades to buy first shows where that reinvested cash does the most work.

A faster session, step by step

  • Collect your offline earnings and reinvest them before doing anything else.
  • Run tight loops: oven, counter, tables, cash piles, drive-thru, repeat.
  • Clear small orders quickly; never cross the shop for a single pizza.
  • Take a multiplier ad once the shop is flowing at full speed.
  • Spend every cash pile the moment a bottleneck upgrade is affordable.

Measure yourself: note your cash, play five focused minutes, and note it again. That per-minute rate is your real score. Every habit in this article — and every upgrade — should move that number. If it does not, something else in the chain needs attention first.

Newer players lose more income to a handful of avoidable habits than to any upgrade choice — Common Beginner Mistakes in Pizza Ready names them. Or return to all articles.

How Pizza Ready Makes Progress While You're Away

Close Pizza Ready!, go to work, sleep, live your life — and when you come back, a pile of cash is waiting. That is the heart of an idle game, and Pizza Ready! leans into it: your pizzeria does not freeze when you leave. This article explains how those offline earnings are worked out, what limits them, and how to arrange your shop so that every hour away pays as much as possible.

What "idle" means in Pizza Ready!

While the game is closed, your shop keeps running in a simplified form. Your hired staff stay at their stations, ovens keep producing, and customers keep being served at a steady rate based on how your shop performs when you play. The game converts that performance into earnings over the time you were gone, and presents the total when you return. You are not watching it happen — the game is crediting you for the business your shop would have done.

Two consequences follow from that design. First, offline income is only as good as the shop you built: a well-staffed, well-upgraded pizzeria earns far more per hour away than a struggling one. Second, your own character is not there. Jobs that only you do — rushing pizzas across the room, clearing a sudden rush — do not happen at full speed while you are away. Staff are the engine of idle income, which is why hiring matters so much more than it first appears.

How offline earnings are calculated

The exact formula is the game's own, but the ingredients are visible in play:

  • Your shop's earning rate. The better your shop performs while you watch it — pizzas served per minute, customers kept happy — the higher the rate the game credits you with while you are gone.
  • Staff coverage. Stations with hired workers keep producing and serving at full pace. Stations that depend on you slow down or stall, dragging the whole rate down.
  • Time away. Earnings grow with the length of your absence, up to a cap (covered below).
  • Production headroom. Ovens and stack space that run dry or overflow quickly in active play also limit how much a shop can notionally sell while unattended.

In short: offline earnings are a snapshot of your shop's health, multiplied by time. Anything that raises your active income per minute raises your idle income too — and anything that creates a bottleneck taxes both.

The offline cap — and why it exists

Idle earnings do not grow forever. Like most idle games, Pizza Ready! caps how much a single absence can pay, so a week away does not hand you a finished empire. Once you hit the cap, extra hours add nothing until you collect. That makes regular check-ins the highest-value habit in the game: collecting twice a day almost always beats collecting once, because the second half of a long absence may have been earning at a capped, wasted rate. Even a one-minute visit — collect, reinvest, close — keeps the meter running at full value.

Maximising what you earn while away

  • Staff every key station before long breaks. A cashier and a chef transform offline earnings, because the register and the ovens are the two stations that must never stop. Our Staff Guide explains hiring order in detail.
  • Remove bottlenecks, not just add power. An idle shop earns at its slowest staffed step. If cooked pizzas pile up in active play because serving lags, that same lag caps your offline rate.
  • Reinvest before you close the game. Spend your cash on the next bottleneck upgrade before a long absence. Cash in the bank earns nothing overnight; an upgraded oven earns all night.
  • Leave full, tidy stations. Clear tables, collect floor cash and make sure stacks are moving before you exit, so the shop you hand over to your staff is in its best working state.
  • Collect on a rhythm. Morning and evening check-ins keep you under the cap and compound faster, because each collection is reinvested and raises the rate for the next stretch.

Should you double your offline earnings?

On return, the game may offer to increase your offline payout in exchange for watching a rewarded ad. Treat it like any other ad offer: its value scales with the payout. Doubling a large overnight collection is usually the best exchange in the game; doubling a small fifteen-minute payout rarely is. If you play in short bursts, consider letting earnings accumulate a little longer before collecting, so that when you do take the offer, it multiplies something worth multiplying. More on using rewarded ads wisely in How to Earn Money Faster in Pizza Ready.

Think of it as rent: your shop pays you for the hours you are gone, and the rent is set by the condition you left it in. Staff it, unblock it, upgrade it, collect regularly — and Pizza Ready! keeps making progress long after you have put the phone down.

Pizza Ready Staff Guide: Who to Hire and Upgrade

You start Pizza Ready! as a one-person business: cook, server, cashier and cleaner in a single pair of shoes. Staff change that. Hired workers hold down stations permanently, keep the shop running while you deal with rushes elsewhere, and — crucially — keep it earning while the game is closed. But hires cost serious cash, and the wrong hire at the wrong time is money standing idle. This guide explains each role, who to bring on first, and how to upgrade your crew as the shop grows.

The roles, explained

  • Cashiers work the registers. They take payment so customers complete their orders without you standing at the counter. A cashier converts the register from a job you must babysit into a station that simply works.
  • Chefs work the kitchen side. They keep pizzas moving off the production line and the finished stack supplied, so the serving side never waits on cooking.
  • Suppliers keep the kitchen stocked and the flow of pizzas coming, supporting the chefs so production does not stall. Think of them as the backstage crew: invisible when things run well, painfully obvious when they are missing and the line slows.
  • Serving helpers, where a location offers them, carry pizzas to tables and the drive-thru, clearing the delivery work that otherwise pulls you away from everything else.

Not every location offers every role at once — new staff types unlock as a shop expands, through the HR office and new areas. The principles below apply whichever roles your current restaurant has open.

Who to hire first: the cashier

For most shops, the first hire should be a cashier. The reasoning is simple: the register is the one station where a customer cannot be helped by anyone else, and every second you spend standing there is a second you are not cooking, carrying or clearing. A cashier frees your character — your most flexible worker — for everything else, and immediately raises both your active serving speed and your offline earnings, because the register now works unattended around the clock. If your queue is short and your real problem is an empty oven stack, a chef can come first instead; the rule underneath the rule is to hire for the station where work waits longest.

Then: chefs and suppliers to feed the line

Once the register is covered, look at the kitchen. If finished pizzas run out while customers wait, hire a chef; if production stutters because the kitchen side cannot keep up with demand, supplier support is what keeps the chefs effective. Kitchen staff pay back fastest in shops where the oven stack is frequently empty — every extra pizza they put into circulation is a pizza you sell within the minute. In shops where pizzas already pile up unsold, kitchen hires can wait; the serving side needs the help instead.

Hire for the bottleneck, upgrade for the rush

Hiring and upgrading solve different problems. A new hire covers a station that currently has nobody — the right move when a whole step of the chain depends on you. An upgrade makes an existing worker faster — the right move when a station is staffed but still falls behind during rushes. A practical order:

  • First, make sure every step of the chain — kitchen, register, serving — has at least one worker who is not you.
  • Next, upgrade the worker at the busiest station. A faster cashier at a permanently queued register earns more than a second worker at a quiet one.
  • Only then add depth: second workers and further levels at the stations that still queue at peak times.

Staff and offline income

Staff are the foundation of idle earnings. While you are away, your character does nothing — your crew does everything. A shop with a cashier, a chef and supplier support keeps producing and selling at a healthy rate all night; a shop where you personally ran the register earns a fraction of that. Before any long break, check that every key station is covered; it is the single biggest lever on what you collect when you return. (How idle progress works explains the full picture.)

Staffing a new location

Each new restaurant starts small again, and early cash is precious. Recreate the same order at a smaller scale: cover the register first, then the kitchen, then deepen. Resist importing your old shop's habits wholesale — a new location's queues are shorter, so one good worker per station goes further than it did in your previous, busier shop. Spend the savings on the capacity and oven upgrades that make those few workers effective; the upgrade buying order pairs naturally with this hiring order.

The thirty-second staffing check: stand back and watch your shop. Any station where work waits with nobody attending it needs a hire. Any station where a worker is present but a queue still grows needs an upgrade. Everything else can wait.

Common Beginner Mistakes in Pizza Ready

Almost every Pizza Ready! player makes the same handful of mistakes in their first shops. None of them feel like mistakes at the time — they feel like being thorough, or saving up, or keeping things tidy. But each one quietly taxes your income, and together they can halve what a shop earns. Here are the big ones, and what to do instead.

Mistake 1: Spreading money across everything

The upgrade menu is long, and the temptation is to buy a little of everything: one level of speed, one of ovens, one of capacity, a decoration of progress everywhere. The problem is that income grows at your bottleneck, and a level spent anywhere else earns nothing until the bottleneck moves. Ten small upgrades spread across the shop can pay back slower than three levels poured into the one station that is actually holding you up. Instead: find the pile-up, spend on it until it clears, then find the next one. Our upgrade order guide walks through the sequence.

Mistake 2: Ignoring upgrades while saving for something big

The mirror-image error: hoarding cash for a distant unlock while your current shop limps along at its starting speed. Cash in the bank earns zero. Every minute spent saving at a slow earning rate makes the big purchase arrive later, not sooner, than if you had bought the cheap upgrades that raise your rate first. Instead: keep a simple rule — if an affordable upgrade clears a visible bottleneck, buy it now. Save deliberately only when the target is close and genuinely transformative, like a new area or a key hire.

Mistake 3: Letting the pizza stack sit at MAX

When the finished-pizza stack reaches its limit, production effectively pauses — the ovens have nowhere to put new pizzas. New players often read a full stack as a good sign ("plenty of pizzas ready!") and go off to clear tables or serve the drive-thru, while the kitchen silently stops earning. Instead: treat MAX as an alarm. Sweep the oven into your arms on every loop around the shop, and if the stack hits the limit often, that is your signal to buy carrying capacity or serving help, not more ovens.

Mistake 4: Maxing one thing and starving the rest

A level-10 oven feeding a level-1 character is a traffic jam with a very fast entrance. Shops earn at the speed of the whole chain — bake, carry, serve, pay — and the chain moves at its slowest link. Instead: upgrade in rounds. Raise one link until it stops being the slowest, then move to the new slowest. Your capacity, speed, ovens and counters should grow up together, roughly in step.

Mistake 5: Leaving cash piles lying around

Customers pay in cash piles left on tables and the floor, and that money does not exist for upgrade purposes until you walk over it. Beginners on a busy loop can leave a small fortune scattered around the shop while wondering why the next upgrade feels unaffordable. Instead: build collection into your route. Design your loop so you pass the tables and counter on the way between oven runs, and finish each session with one full sweep of the floor.

Mistake 6: Hiring late — or hiring randomly

Some beginners treat staff as a luxury for later, and run every station themselves long past the point where one pair of hands is the shop's ceiling. Others hire whoever is cheapest the moment the HR office opens, regardless of where work actually waits. Both cost money: the first caps your active and offline income; the second parks wages at a quiet station while a busy one drowns. Instead: hire as soon as a station regularly waits for you — cashier first in most shops — and always staff the bottleneck. The Staff Guide covers roles and upgrade priorities in full.

Mistake 7: Forgetting the shop earns while you're away

New players often close the game mid-chaos: tables uncleared, cash uncollected, a station unstaffed, and a pocketful of unspent earnings. Your offline income is based on the shop you leave behind, so a messy exit means a poorer return. Instead: spend sixty seconds before closing — collect everything, buy the next bottleneck upgrade, confirm each key station has a worker. Then collect again when you come back, and reinvest before you do anything else. (How idle earnings work explains why this pays so well.)

Mistake 8: Grinding a finished shop instead of moving on

When a location's goals are complete, its remaining upgrades get expensive and its growth slows to a crawl — by design. Lingering because the shop feels comfortable delays the fresh, cheap, fast-paying growth of the next restaurant. Instead: once the star bar is full and the next location is open, move. Everything you learned goes with you, and early upgrades in a new shop are the best-value purchases in the game.

The common thread: every mistake on this list is the same mistake — money, pizzas or attention sitting idle somewhere it cannot earn. Keep cash invested, stacks moving, stations staffed and yourself looping, and a beginner shop starts performing like a veteran one surprisingly fast.

Ready to put it into practice? Start with How to Earn Money Faster in Pizza Ready, or browse all articles.

Unlocking New Shops in Pizza Ready: How It Works

Your first pizzeria is only the beginning. Pizza Ready! is built as a journey from one small restaurant to a chain of them, and every new location is where the game's biggest growth lives. But how exactly does a new shop unlock, what do you keep when you move on, and how do you know whether it is time to expand or to keep improving the restaurant you already have? This guide answers all three questions.

How a new location unlocks

Each restaurant tracks its own completion through the star progress bar at the top of the screen. As you serve customers and complete the location's listed goals — things like reaching certain upgrade levels, opening new areas of the shop and serving enough guests — the bar fills. When a location's goals are complete, the next restaurant becomes available and you can travel to it and start building there.

Two things are worth understanding about that bar. First, it rewards balanced progress: the goals usually touch several parts of the shop, so a restaurant with maxed ovens but no staff and no seating will stall before the finish line. Second, finishing a location is not about buying literally everything it offers. Some of the most expensive late upgrades in a shop are optional polish; the goals are the checklist that matters, and they are designed to be completed while the shop still has headroom to grow.

What carries over to the new shop — and what does not

Moving to a new location is a fresh start for the building, not for you as a player:

  • Your knowledge carries over. This sounds like a joke, but it is the biggest carry-over of all. You already know the buying order, the hiring order and the loops that work, so a new shop reaches in an hour what your first shop took a day to reach.
  • Premium items and cosmetics carry over. Things tied to your account rather than to one restaurant — such as purchased ad removal and unlocked skins — stay with you.
  • The old shop stays yours. Moving on does not demolish your previous restaurant. You can travel back to earlier locations, and they remain part of your chain.
  • Cash and upgrades do not transfer. Each location has its own economy. The cash pile and upgraded ovens in shop one do not move to shop two — the new restaurant starts with small numbers and cheap upgrades, exactly like your first day, but at a bigger scale as the chain progresses.
  • Staff are hired per location. Your crew in one restaurant does not follow you to the next. Each new shop needs its own cashiers and chefs, hired with that shop's own earnings.

Because nothing financial transfers, there is no benefit to hoarding cash in a finished shop "for later." Money left unspent in a completed location is money that stops working. Spend it on that shop's remaining goals, or move on.

Expand or upgrade? How to decide

The most common question mid-game is whether to keep pouring cash into the current restaurant or push through its final goals and open the next one. A few rules of thumb make the decision easy:

  • Expand when the goals are nearly done. If the star bar is close to full, finish it. The last goals are usually the fastest route to the new location, and a new shop's early upgrades are the best-value purchases in the game — cheap, quick and immediately profitable.
  • Upgrade when a bottleneck is blocking the goals themselves. If you cannot complete a goal because customers queue faster than you can serve them, that is not a reason to delay expansion — it is the upgrade the goal is asking for. Buy the fix, finish the goal, then move.
  • Expand when upgrade prices have ballooned. Late upgrades in an old shop cost a fortune for small percentage gains. When the next level of anything costs more than your shop earns in several minutes, compare it honestly with a fresh location, where the same cash buys level after level of everything.
  • Upgrade when the shop still feels cheap to improve. Early and mid-game in a location, upgrades pay back in minutes. There is no prize for rushing to a new city with a half-built shop behind you if the current one still grows every time you spend.

Your first hour in a new shop

A new location replays the opening of the game — one oven, a counter, your own two hands — but you are not a beginner anymore. Recreate your proven order quickly: carrying capacity and speed for yourself, a cashier as soon as the register queues, oven output once you can move what it makes, then counters, tables and the drive-thru as each one starts to queue. The upgrade buying order and Staff Guide apply in a new shop exactly as they did in your first; only the numbers are bigger.

The short version: fill the star bar to unlock the next shop, expect to rebuild the business (not your account) when you get there, and let upgrade prices make the decision for you — cheap growth means stay, expensive inches mean it is time to expand.

One trap to avoid in all of this is grinding a finished shop long past its prime — it is on our list of common beginner mistakes. Or return to all articles.

How to Play Pizza Ready on PC

Pizza Ready! is made for phones and tablets, and Supercent publishes it on Google Play and the Apple App Store — there is no official Windows or Mac version, and no official download for PC exists. Even so, plenty of players would like their pizzeria on a bigger screen. This article explains the options honestly: which ones are legitimate, which ones to avoid, and whether a bigger screen actually helps an idle game like this one.

The honest starting point

Any website offering a "Pizza Ready PC download," an installer, or a modified version of the game for computers is unofficial. At best those files are repackaged copies distributed without permission; at worst they bundle adware or malware, which is a common trick with popular free games. The same goes for APK sites that claim to offer a special PC edition. The genuine game comes from exactly two places: Google Play and the App Store. Everything below works within that rule.

Option 1: Google Play Games on PC

Google offers an official way to play many Android games on Windows: Google Play Games on PC. It is Google's own program, you sign in with the same Google account you use on your phone, and games are downloaded through it just like on mobile. If Pizza Ready! is available in the catalogue in your region, this is the cleanest route to a big screen: official software, official game build, and progress tied to your account. Availability varies by country and by title, so check the catalogue rather than assuming — and if the game is not listed there yet, that is Google's rollout decision, not something a third-party site can fix for you.

Option 2: Android emulators — with eyes open

An Android emulator is software that runs a virtual Android phone on your computer, inside which you can open Google Play and install games normally. Well-known emulators are a long-standing, legitimate category of software, and installing the game from the real Play Store inside one is very different from downloading a random "PC version." Still, go in with clear eyes:

  • Download the emulator only from its maker's official website. Emulator names are frequently copied by download portals that add unwanted extras to the installer.
  • Expect ads and bundled offers. Free emulators are businesses; many show ads or promote sponsored apps. That is normal, but decline anything extra offered during setup.
  • Performance varies. Pizza Ready! is a light game, so most modern PCs run it smoothly, but very old machines can struggle with emulation overhead.
  • Support is limited. The game is designed and tested for real phones. If something behaves oddly in an emulator, the developer's support is aimed at mobile devices.

Option 3: Mirror your phone to your monitor

If you simply want a bigger view, you may not need the game on the PC at all. Both Android and iPhone can mirror their screens to many TVs and monitors, and Windows and Mac can display a phone's screen through built-in or bundled tools. The game still runs on your phone — where it is fully official and your progress lives — while you watch and tap on a larger display. For short check-in sessions this is overkill, but for a long active session at a desk it is the zero-risk option: nothing extra to install on the game side, nothing unofficial anywhere.

Does a bigger screen actually help an idle game?

Honestly? Less than you might expect, and it is worth saying so. Pizza Ready! earns most of its money while you are not playing — that is the point of the genre, and your shop progresses the same whether it sits on a phone or a 27-inch monitor (see how idle progress works). Where a PC setup genuinely helps:

  • Long active sessions are more comfortable. During events or a focused push to finish a location, a big screen and a mouse make the loop easier on your eyes and hands.
  • Everything is easier to read. Upgrade menus, goal lists and prices are simply clearer at monitor size.
  • Your phone stays free. The game can tick along on the PC while your phone charges or handles calls and messages.

And where it does not help:

  • No earnings advantage. Income rates, offline caps and upgrade prices are identical. A PC is a display choice, not a boost.
  • Check-ins are slower. The highest-value habit in an idle game is the one-minute collect-and-reinvest visit, and nothing beats a phone in your pocket for that. Booting a PC or emulator for a 60-second check-in usually means the check-in stops happening.
  • Touch is the native control. The game is built around quick taps and drags; a mouse works, but it is a translation, not an improvement.

Keeping your progress safe

Whichever screen you play on, protect the account behind the game. Sign in with your Google or Apple account in the official app so your progress is tied to you rather than to one device, use the same account if you try Google Play Games on PC, and never enter your account details into a third-party "PC version," a mod, or a site promising free currency — those are the classic routes to a stolen account, and no shortcut is worth a pizzeria you spent months building.

Bottom line: there is no official Pizza Ready! for PC, and any site claiming otherwise is not offering the real thing. Google Play Games on PC is the official route where available; a reputable emulator running the real Play Store build, or simply mirroring your phone, are the sensible alternatives. Play on the big screen for comfort — just keep collecting on your phone, because that is where idle games are won.

Pizza Ready! FAQ

The questions new players ask most, answered straight.

Is Pizza Ready! free to play?
Yes. Pizza Ready! is free to download and play on Android and iPhone. The game is supported by ads and offers optional in-app purchases, such as removing ads, but everything needed to progress can be earned by playing.
Where can I download Pizza Ready! safely?
Only from the official stores: Google Play for Android and the Apple App Store for iPhone and iPad. The publisher is Supercent. Avoid third-party APK or mod sites — they are unofficial and can be unsafe.
Who makes Pizza Ready!?
Pizza Ready! is developed and published by Supercent, Inc., a mobile game studio based in Seoul, South Korea, known for casual idle and simulation games.
Can I play Pizza Ready! offline?
Yes, the core game works offline. Your shop keeps producing and earning while you are away, and you collect the income when you return. An internet connection is needed for ads, purchases and some events.
How do I earn money faster in Pizza Ready!?
Keep your ovens stocked so pizzas never stop coming out, upgrade your carrying capacity and movement speed early, hire cashiers and chefs as soon as you can afford them, and collect the cash piles on the floor regularly so customers keep flowing. Our Tips & Tricks page goes deeper.
What should I upgrade first?
Start with your own capacity and speed, then oven output. After that, unlock extra tables and registers, and hire staff for the stations you visit most often. Balance upgrades instead of maxing one thing while everything else stays slow.
How do I hire staff in Pizza Ready!?
As your shop grows you unlock an HR office where you can recruit chefs, cashiers and other helpers with the cash you earn. Staff keep their stations running automatically, including while you focus on other tasks.
How do I expand to new locations?
Complete the goals in your current shop to fill its star progress bar. Finishing a location unlocks the next restaurant, where you build the business up again with everything you have learned, at a bigger scale.
What devices does Pizza Ready! need?
On iPhone and iPad it requires iOS 15.0 or later. On Android it runs on most phones with Android 7.0 or later. The game is a few hundred megabytes, so keep some free storage space.
Is this website the official Pizza Ready! site?
No. This is an unofficial fan guide made by players. It is not affiliated with or endorsed by Supercent. Pizza Ready! and its artwork belong to Supercent, and downloads are handled by Google Play and the App Store. See our Disclaimer.
